content: Deceleration refers to the slowing down of blood flow within an artery at any point during its course. The deceleration time of diastolic flow is a parameter that can be used to assess the extent of microvascular damage. This damage may serve as a predictor of residual myocardial viability, which is often evaluated through angiography. Microvascular ischemic injury, which occurs following the occlusion of an epicardial coronary artery, leads to increased coronary vascular resistance. This resistance is partly due to perivascular edema and the formation of capillary leukocyte plugs, which impede the full restoration of myocardial perfusion. In this context, the deceleration time of diastolic flow velocity reflects the degree of ischemic microvascular impairment. This impairment significantly influences total coronary resistance, even in patients who do not have severe coronary stenosis. For instance, in cases of no-reflow, there is a reduction in postprocedural coronary systolic flow velocity, which correlates with an increase in total coronary resistance. The deceleration time of diastolic flow velocity, therefore, provides insight into coronary blood flow and is indicative of the ratio of perfused myocardium to functioning coronary microvasculature. In viable myocardium, the coronary blood flow velocity pattern appears nearly normal. However, in nonviable myocardium, this pattern is altered due to the presence of systolic retrograde flow and a rapid deceleration of diastolic flow velocity. These changes are indicative of microvascular damage and can predict the extent of residual myocardial viability. Clinically, the coronary blood flow velocity pattern in patients with reperfused acute myocardial infarction (AMI) and no-reflow is characterized by several features: The presence of systolic retrograde flow. A reduction in systolic antegrade flow. A rapid deceleration of diastolic flow velocity. These disturbances may occur immediately after reperfusion or shortly thereafter. Additionally, abnormalities during the deceleration phase of systole are often associated with mild to moderate coronary stenosis.
